topic: The Zeigarnik effect: do unfinished tasks really haunt you?
title: Do Unfinished Tasks Really Haunt You?
voiceover: Why do unfinished tasks nag at you? In the 1920s, psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik reported that people remembered interrupted tasks better than completed ones. That became known as the Zeigarnik effect. But a 2025 meta-analysis found no memory advantage for unfinished tasks. An earlier replication attempt by Annie van Bergen in 1968 had also failed to find one. Unfinished goals can still keep intruding on your thoughts, though. Psychologists Masicampo and Baumeister showed that making a specific plan for a goal eliminated those effects. In one study, the people who later carried out their plans were the ones whose intrusive thoughts stopped. So instead of just listing a task, decide exactly when and where you will start. Tomorrow: why does losing hurt more than winning feels good?

description: Do unfinished tasks really stick in memory? A 2025 meta-analysis found no memory advantage, but unfinished goals can still intrude on your thoughts, and a specific plan can quiet them. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Masicampo, E. J., & Baumeister, R. F. (2011). Consider it done! Plan making can eliminate the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(4), 667-683. Source: Ghibellini, R., & Meier, B. (2025). Interruption, recall and resumption: A meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (Palgrave Communications), 12.
accuracy_note: Zeigarnik's original memory claim has failed to replicate (Van Bergen 1968; Ghibellini & Meier 2025 meta-analysis). Masicampo & Baumeister (2011) studied goal-related intrusive thoughts in lab tasks, not everyday to-do lists.
